description:
Gray Fox or Domestic Cat?

These are old tracks but they were made in soft clay. See how the second photo shows a slightly swirled track with tiny claws registering for toes 3 and 4.

The third photo shows a total of four tracks, including the first two. There are raccoon tracks in the photo as well, but they all point down and the fox tracks point up.

I originally thought these were fox tracks, but now I'm leaning towards Domestic Cat based on  a couple things. The distance between the claw marks and the toe pads on the second photo is too short for Gray Fox. And the toe pads are too spread out and long. I'm having trouble seeing enough detail in the palm pads to use those to tell.

What do you guys think?

Identification: 
This species is clearly a member of the family, Felidae. It has a long tail, gracile body, and retractable claws.

Because I know that this is obviously a domestic cat based on its small body size, simple coloration, quadrupedal locomotion and whiskers, I place this specimen in the genus Felis, species silvestris and subspecies catus. This particular subspecies distinguishes from other wild cats and is commonly known as the domesticated or feral cat. 

Conditions: Most of these cats are known to be nocturnal, so it makes sense that I saw these cats later at night. It was cold, the low that day was reported to be in the 50’s. There was no humidity, and it hadn’t rained that day. 

Location: Found on my way coming back from Library West. I’ve seen feral cats in this general location before. When I tried to get closer to take a picture, the cat ran into the sewage drain alongside the parking lot. When I got closer, I could see another cat in the drain as well. I believe that this is where a lot of these feral cats live because it is a good place to escape from larger predators. 

Behavior: The cat was very scared of humans. The first time I tried to get closer it would crouch down, back up and run away. Every time it stopped, it would crouch down and lock its gaze on me. After a while, it ran into the gutter to escape me.

description: When I saw this cat I was at my apartment complex (Towne Parc) at night so it was pretty cool outside. We have a lot of stray cats, especially next to my apartment since it’s near some woods, so they’ll come in and out of the woods and walk around the parking lot. Thanks to the lecture in lab and what I already know about cats, I know this organism is in order carnivora. This cat is terrestrial with long, sharp claws. And having done a lot of dental cleanings on cats I know their canines are well developed and adapted for meat-eating. (Another word for cat being feline, I know this mammal is in family Felidae and subfamily Felinae but we did not cover this in class/lab).

description:
This cat is extremely aggressive towards the other stray and feral cats that have turned up here, and kept chasing the grey and white cat we've nicknamed Cutie Baby. We had to pick her up to keep him away from her, and even then he kept advancing aggressively.

I think there might be something wrong with his eyes, he was acting like he couldn't see very well, and he has scratches on his face near his eyes.

This seems to be yet another black cat that is separate from the other one I saw here before that had the white hourglass on its chest. sigh. apparently our appartment has just become a dumping ground for unwanted cats.

This one was moderately shy of us, it seemed to care mostly about being near "Cutie Baby" as we're calling her. When she started approaching us, this one followed her up until about 20ft, when it sat down and waited. A few times it seemed like it wanted to approach, but never did. When our neighbor came outside and Cutie Baby ran to greet her, this cat again followed, but then hung back out of reach.

Our neighbor told us "Cutie Baby" was abandoned by another one of our neighbors when they moved away, and that this happens a lot here. She also told us there are foxes that come through later in the year and eat most of the cats.

so.

if anyone in the Savannah area or anyone willing to drive here wants a free cat (or two, this one and Cutie Baby since they get along), let me know. We can't adopt them ourselves or even "foster" them beacuse we're at the limit for cats we're allowed to have in our appartment, but if you are willing to take them, we can definitely catch "Cutie Baby" and it probably wouldn't be too difficult to catch this one as well. It's shy, but not terrified, and it would probably be very easy to socialize it.

(Despite what most people think, it is 100% a myth that it's impossible to socialize adult cats. I know from experience. The more skittish the cat is, the longer it'll take to gain their trust, but that doesn't mean it's impossible.)

Here is the observation for Cutie Baby, this one's friend: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/115665890

This observation is meant to show this kitten's last "feral" location. This was the first picture we took of her after we caught her, because before we caught her it was too dark outside to get pictures.

How did we catch her, you ask? Did we use a live catch trap? No, we were kids who didn't have any money. Instead I took a wire coat hanger, unbent it, and tied one end to the door of an old cat carrier, put a bowl of food in it, and then sat out on the porch in the dark waiting for the cats to show up. Dani went in, I closed the door, and she was caught.

For the other cats, I improved a box trap by wiring two cardboard boxes together so that one on top could be dropped down onto the one below to close it, with slots in the sides to let in air and light. I put a stack of newspapers on top so it would be weighted enough to fall and stay down, and tied a string to the top which I looped over a hook for hanging plants, then held onto the other end, this time sitting just inside the screen door, to keep the top lifted up.

Dani and Merlin, her brother and mother, were easy to catch this way.

Her father, Jessi, not so much. He decided to stick his paws through the slots in the side to pick food out, lol. But eventually he went in.

Where there's a will, there's a way.

We still have Dani in 2022, she's eight years old now, and now living with us all the way in Savannah Georgia, along with her brother.

This observation should not be marked captive/cultivated, because this is meant to show her last wild location.

She, along with her brother, mother, and father were caught in October 2014, though I don't have the exact dates we caught the other three.

Please keep your cats inside. They will be happier, safer, and even more importantly, domestic cats are an invasive species /no matter where you live on this planet/. Domestic cats are responsible for over 60 species going extinct /so far/, and that alone is a tragedy that should never have happened. Don't let that number get any higher. Keep your cats inside, or walk them on a leash or buy a catio. Your cat does not need to be outside to be happy. They are not wild animals, they are domesticated. Even feral cats are better off either being brought inside or euthanized. They will do nothing but suffer outside, and decimate native wildlife before they die an early, most likely painful death.

description: Either a stray or feral. Though also a grey tabby, this is a different individual to the other one that I have noted previously In this location.

Three grey tabby cats, stray or feral. 

Cat #1 Is an adult female which has been sighted repeatedly at this location for at least 5 months. 

I first observed cat #2 just over 2 weeks prior to this observation. They are markedly more small than cats #1 and #3 and may be a juvenile. They exhibit more apprehensive behavior around humans. Though they have gotten progressively closer to nearby humans since their initial appearance, they still avoid direct human context and it is unknown if they are male or female at this time. 

Cat 1 appears domineering over 2, always being the first to take morsels of food when they approach at the same time.  The smaller cat attempted to initiate gentle physical contact with their larger companion several times, the latter of which responded to this unfavorably. This appeared to be a dominant and boundary-setting behavior rather than an attempt at serious injury or agression.

Cat #3 first appeared to me today. They are closer in size to cat #1 but share the characteristic cheek-tufts of 2, perhaps suggesting a genetic relation. They reacted favorably to human contact, voluntarily nuzzling into a hand when offered one. However, the unexpected nature of the encounter elicited a strong observer response that precluded comprehensive study of its reproductive anatomy. Due to this as well as poor lighting conditions, cat #3 is also of currently unknown sex. This cat was observed repeatedly vocalizing back and forth with cat 1, while the smallest of the three stayed mostly silent.
